questions.stem: What is the term used to describe the quantity of matter present in an object?
questions.solution: Mass is the term used to describe the quantity of matter present in an object. Weight is a measure of the force of gravity acting on an object, volume is the space an object occupies, and density is the amount of mass in a given volume.

questions.stem: If you add more salt to a solution that already contains dissolved salt, what will happen if the solution is saturated?
choices: The salt will continue to dissolve completely
The salt will start to dissolve partially
The salt will not dissolve and settle at the bottom
questions.solution: A saturated solution is one in which the maximum amount of solute has already been dissolved. Adding more salt to such a solution will not cause it to dissolve further, so it will remain as solid at the bottom. The other options are incorrect because they suggest dissolution or evaporation, which do not occur in a saturated solution.

questions.stem: A student dissolves 10 g of sugar in 50 mL of water. What is the solubility of sugar in water based on this?
questions.solution: Solubility is defined as the maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved in 100 mL of solvent. If 10 g of sugar dissolves in 50 mL, then 20 g would dissolve in 100 mL, making 20 g per 100 mL the correct answer. The other options are incorrect calculations based on the given data.

questions.stem: A student adds salt to water and notices that after some time, the salt no longer dissolves and settles at the bottom. What does this indicate about the solution?
questions.solution: When salt stops dissolving and settles at the bottom, it means the solution has reached its maximum capacity to dissolve the salt. This is the definition of a saturated solution. An unsaturated solution would still be able to dissolve more salt, a concentrated solution refers to the amount of solute, and a dilute solution has very little solute, none of which match the observed behavior.

questions.stem: A student added 20 g of salt to 100 mL of water at room temperature and found that not all the salt dissolved. What can be concluded from this observation?
questions.solution: A saturated solution is one in which no more solute can be dissolved at a given temperature. Since not all the salt dissolved, the solution has reached its maximum capacity for dissolving salt, making it a saturated solution. questions.stem: A student adds 50 g of salt to 100 mL of water at room temperature, and all the salt dissolves. What type of solution is this?
questions.solution: The correct answer is Unsaturated. An unsaturated solution is one in which more solute can still be dissolved at a given temperature, which matches the situation where all the salt dissolved and more could still be added. A saturated solution would not allow any more solute to dissolve, a supersaturated solution contains more solute than normally possible, and a colloid is a mixture where particles are dispersed but not dissolved.

questions.stem: A student made a sugar solution by dissolving sugar in water. The solution was then divided into two parts. One part was kept at room temperature, and the other was heated. Which part will have a higher solubility of sugar?
questions.solution: Heating increases the solubility of most solid solutes in water. Therefore, the heated solution will have a higher solubility of sugar. The solubility of a solute is affected by temperature, and for most solids, solubility increases with temperature.

questions.stem: A student wants to determine if a soil sample contains soluble substances. Which of the following properties should be compared between the soil and the tap water?
questions.solution: The correct answer is 'density'. If the soil contains soluble substances, dissolving them in water will change the density of the water. Other properties like pH, temperature, and light scattering may not be as reliable indicators of soluble substances. pH could change, but it is not the most definitive measure. Temperature is not directly affected by soluble substances. Light scattering may vary but is not a direct indicator of solubility. Therefore, comparing the density of the water before and after the soil is added is the best method to determine if there are soluble substances in the soil.

questions.stem: A student dissolved 5 g of salt in 100 mL of water and found that all the salt dissolved. The student then added another 5 g of salt, and again all the salt dissolved. What can be concluded about the solution?
questions.solution: The solution is unsaturated because it can still dissolve more solute. A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute, and a supersaturated solution contains more solute than it should at a given temperature. A colloid is a different type of mixture where particles are dispersed but not dissolved.

questions.stem: Why does ice float on water?
choices: Because it is colder than liquid water
Because its density is higher than liquid water
Because it is less dense than liquid water
Because it is made of pure water
questions.solution: The correct answer is 'Because it is less dense than liquid water'. When water freezes into ice, its molecules form a crystalline structure that takes up more space, making ice less dense than liquid water. This lower density allows ice to float on the surface of water. The other options are incorrect because colder temperature alone does not explain buoyancy, and the density of ice is lower, not higher, than that of liquid water. The purity of water is not the reason for ice floating.

questions.stem: Why is a 100 mL measuring cylinder the best choice to measure 70 mL of water?
choices: It is the most widely available
questions.solution: A 100 mL measuring cylinder is the most accurate for measuring 70 mL because it has markings that allow for precise measurement within that range. Larger cylinders have wider intervals between markings, making it harder to measure smaller volumes accurately. Smaller cylinders would require multiple measurements, which increases the chance of error. The other options—convenience, cost, and availability—are not directly related to the precision of the measurement.
